title: Laws and files a lobbyist’s client asked about, matched by file number
question: For each Board file a lobbyist named by number: who was the client, who was contacted, who sponsored it, what happened, and did the lobbyist’s circle give to the sponsors?
finding: 294 Board files are named by number in lobbyists’ reports and 216 of them passed. Where every client sought support, 84.1% of 132 files passed; where every client was opposed, 58.1% of 31 passed; 4 had clients on both sides. The clients paid the firms involved $12.8 million in the years of those contacts. For 28 files the circle of a lobbying client or firm gave to a sponsor’s committees in the two years before introduction or while the file was pending ($53,901 in all). A final Board roll call is on disk for 215 of the 294 files: 191 had no vote against and 24 were divided; on 1 the motion failed. 5 of the roll calls were read from the Clerk’s minutes because the vote page lists no member, and for 1 more file the Board voted but neither source settles how each member voted.
how: A contact is tied to a file only by the six-digit Board file number the lobbyist wrote, with the contact dated from two years before to three years after introduction. Outcome, sponsors and dates are the Board’s own record; a file sponsored by “Mayor” is credited to the mayoral candidate whom lobbyists most often reported contacting at the Mayor’s office in both the year before and the year after that date, and to nobody where the two differ (a change of mayor). Fees are all payments from those clients to those firms in the calendar years of the contacts, whatever they were for. Circle giving is contributions from the lobbyists, their firms, colleagues, the clients and the clients’ officers to the sponsor’s committees. The final vote is the Board’s last roll call on the measure itself (adopted, approved, passed on first reading or finally passed; a vote to submit a charter amendment to the voters is not among them), read from the Board’s roll-call pages for every file a lobbyist cited by number, 2015 to November 2026; the members voting no are named, and the divided votes are set out member by member in the screen on divided votes. A file with no final vote shown never reached one in those pages or was decided before 2015. Where the vote page lists no member, the votes are taken from the Clerk’s published minutes of the same meeting and the row says so; a vote that neither source records member by member is marked as such and never counted as unanimous. Rows are ordered by circle giving to sponsors, then by contacts.
limits: Lobbying is registered, and so is giving by a lobbyist’s clients and colleagues. An official can sponsor or vote for something a donor wants because the official already favoured it; a donor can give to an official because of what the official already stands for. Passing is the normal fate of a Board file, so a high pass rate among lobbied files shows little; files that every client opposed still passed 58.1% of the time, and many contacts only “monitor”. The same fee can sit beside several files. A client’s officers give to candidates for reasons unconnected to one file. For 4 files the status on record is not “Passed” although the final roll call carried (Filed, Mayors Office, Pending Committee Action, Unfinished Business-Final Passage): a measure can pass the Board and still await signature or be vetoed, and the notes with the roll-call pages say the status copy on disk for files of 2014 to 2018 is an older one. Those files count as not passed in the shares above. For 332 roll calls the Clerk’s vote page says “by the following vote” and lists no member, 306 of them dated 2016-04-13 to 2016-07-26; 315 were read instead from the vote lines in the Clerk’s published minutes of the same meeting, and 17 remain without member votes and are counted nowhere here. 2 files (160358, 160657) are left out wherever a final vote is counted or tested: for their last passage vote the vote page lists no member and the minutes print the action twice with different tallies, so it is not counted as unanimous and no earlier reading stands in for it. A private payment for an official act cannot be seen in any of these records, and nothing here says one was made. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
